extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (Office personnel) and patent practitioners/prosecutors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and documenting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, implementing Graham factors and the Supreme Court's KSR principles; covers claim scope, prior art search, level of ordinary skill, rationales for obviousness, applicant replies, and rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103 statutory standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained ... if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes statutory subsections (a)-(c) (and biotech/process provisions). Serves as the fundamental legal standard against which obviousness is judged; rejections must be based on substantive law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use KSR flexible approach (avoid rigid TSM)
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR reaffirmed framework from Graham but criticized an overly rigid TSM test; examiners should apply a flexible, common-sense approach to providing reasons for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR cautions against strict confines (e.g., looking only to the patent's stated problem) and emphasizes that common sense, predictable variations, and ordinary creativity are relevant. Examiners should give reasoned explanations that avoid conclusory generalizations; TSM remains a valid rationale when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries — scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the scope and content of the prior art is a primary factual inquiry for obviousness under Graham v. John Deere Co.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must thoroughly understand the disclosed invention (read specification and claims) and determine the claimed scope (broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification). Use MPEP §§904, 2111 as guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries — differences between claimed invention and prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art is a required factual inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires interpreting claim language (see MPEP §2111) and considering the invention and prior art as a whole (see MPEP §2141.02). The mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness; explain why differences matter to obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries — level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art is a factual inquiry relevant to obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding as to level of ordinary skill should be included explicitly or implicitly in view of the prior art applied. Consider factors (type of problems, prior art solutions, rapidity of innovations, sophistication of technology, educational level of active workers). Examiners may rely on their expertise or evidence of record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of objective evidence (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence relevant to obviousness (commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, unexpected results) must be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be in the specification, filed with the application, or presented later; weight is case-by-case and not dispositive by mere presentation. See Graham factors and MPEP on secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel must act as factfinders and articulate findings of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel fulfill the role of factfinder for Graham inquiries and must include findings of fact concerning state of the art and teachings of applied references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual findings (e.g., how a person of ordinary skill would understand a reference) are necessary underpinnings for legal conclusions. 35 U.S.C. 132 requires notifying applicant of reasons for rejection; clearly setting forth findings and rationales aids resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope determined by broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Phillips v. AWH Corp. and MPEP §2111. Determination of claim scope informs what to search and what references can read on the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for — claimed subject matter and disclosed features
rubrics_metrics.description: The search should cover the claimed subject matter and should also cover the disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching/suggestion to combine, preferred searches will seek references that provide such teaching/suggestion if they exist. See MPEP §904.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search — field of endeavor and reasonably pertinent art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art for 35 U.S.C. 103 can be either in the field of applicant’s endeavor or be reasonably pertinent to the particular problem with which the applicant was concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include prior art from other fields when reasonably pertinent; consider market forces/design incentives prompting variations across fields (KSR). Follow MPEP §§904–904.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining differences requires interpreting claim language and considering whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining differences between the claimed invention and prior art requires interpreting the claim language and considering both invention and prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP §2111 and §2141.02; differences must be explained in context of claim construction and total disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate/resolve level of ordinary skill when making obviousness rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Any obviousness rejection should include, explicitly or implicitly, an indication of the level of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A level finding may be used as a partial basis for obviousness. Use In re GPAC and related cases for factors. If prior art itself reflects appropriate level, separate specification of level may be unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill is of ordinary creativity (not an automaton)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of ordinary skill in the art is also a person of ordinary creativity, able to fit teachings together and employ inferences and creative steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR emphasizes that such a person can combine teachings like puzzle pieces; examiners may consider inferences and creative steps that a person of ordinary skill would employ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales for supporting a rejection must be clearly articulated (no conclusory statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; 'there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit analysis and rationale (citation to KSR and In re Kahn). Avoid unsupported generalizations; explain why differences would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale A — Combining prior art elements by known methods yielding predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results is a valid rationale for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when combination would perform as expected and produce predictable outcome; see examples in MPEP §2143/§2144.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale B — Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results supports obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies when substituted element is known in the field and yields expected function without more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale C — Use of known technique to improve similar devices in same way
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a known technique to improve similar devices (methods or products) in the same way may render an invention obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person of ordinary skill would recognize the technique's applicability to similar devices, obviousness may follow unless application is beyond skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale D — Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results supports obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus is on devices 'ready for improvement' where application of known methods would be predictable to skilled artisans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale E — 'Obvious to try' with finite, predictable solutions and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success, an 'obvious to try' rationale may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cautiously; KSR recognized 'obvious to try' as valid where solutions are finite and predictable; must articulate expectation of success, not merely speculative experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale F — Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in another
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations for use in the same or different field if variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR noted that design incentives and market forces can make cross-field variations predictable; consider analogous/nonanalogous art analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale G — Teaching, suggestion, or motivation in prior art to modify/combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references is a recognized rationale for obviousness (TSM-related).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although KSR criticized rigid application, TSM is still a valid line of reasoning; include explicit explanation where used. See MPEP §2143.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explicit findings on how a person of ordinary skill would have understood/acted
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain circumstances, it may be important to include explicit findings as to how a person of ordinary skill would have understood prior art teachings or what such a person would have known or could have done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factual findings bolster the rationale for obviousness and should be reflected in Office actions where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply requirements under 37 C.F.R. 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant must distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replies must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable. A traverse must include reasoned statements explaining why the examiner erred; mere conclusory assertions are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective traverse requires reasoned statement, not mere assertion of lack of prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant disagrees with factual findings, an effective traverse must include reasoned explanation why the Office erred; mere statements that the Office hasn't established a prima facie case or that common knowledge is unsupported are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If traverse is insufficient, examiner may repeat rejection and make next Office action final (see MPEP §706.07(a)). Examiners should identify deficiencies in applicant responses when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's timely rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence that is timely presented by applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations; examiners must weigh such evidence and address it in re-evaluation. Timeliness and materiality affect consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away and its importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art teachings that criticize, discredit, or otherwise discourage the claimed solution indicate 'teaching away' and weigh against obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples (e.g., W.L. Gore v. Garlock) where prior art taught away. Note that mere disclosure of multiple alternatives does not equal teaching away (see In re Fulton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere disclosure of multiple alternatives does not teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art’s mere disclosure of more than one alternative does not constitute teaching away because such disclosure does not criticize or discredit any alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between an explicit discouragement (teaching away) and simple listing of alternatives; analysis must explain why a reference does or does not teach away (see In re Fulton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying particular level of skill not required if prior art reflects level
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only facts of record pertaining to level of skill are found within the prior art of record, an invention may be held obvious without a specific finding of a particular level of skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (Chore-Time, Okajima) permits reliance on prior art to reflect appropriate skill level; however, examiners must ensure objectivity and appropriate factual underpinnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-prior art documents to show level of ordinary skill or motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: References that postdate the claimed invention or were not widely disseminated (thus not prior art) may nevertheless be used to demonstrate the level of ordinary skill or motivation to combine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include engineer drawings or later documents used to show implicit motivations or skill level (see Ex parte Erlich; National Steel Car Ltd. v. Canadian Pacific Railway).
